Unit 4, The Roaring Twenties

Douglas County Courthouse, Omaha, the morning after the mob. September 1919

Section 1

What Was the Red Summer of 1919?

In 1919 racial violence swept the country. and , set off by rumors and accusations, broke out in Northern cities, across the South, in the cotton country of Arkansas and in the nation's capital. Most were called at the time, and the word still hides what they were: white attacks on Black communities. It happened in something like three dozen places that year, and the reason was rarely hidden. Black Southerners had moved North and taken jobs, and Black veterans were beginning to stand up for themselves. Newspapers and the federal government preferred a different explanation and blamed agitators for stirring Black Americans up.

This was the year the soldiers came home. On February 17, 1919, the 369th Infantry, the regiment the French called the Hellfighters, marched up Fifth Avenue and into Harlem while hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers came out to cheer them. By July, white servicemen were pulling Black veterans off streetcars and beating them in the street four blocks from the White House. These men had spent a year being told they were risking their lives for democracy. They came home expecting some of it, and what met them instead was a wave of horrific racial violence that would later be called the .

Start with the roots. Then work the map, one stop at a time, and watch where the country fills in. Chicago is on this page too, but it is one stop out of thirteen. Any word with a dotted underline will give you a definition if you click it.

Section 2

The Roots of Red Summer

Nothing in 1919 came out of nowhere. Click each factor.

A family on the road north, from the Great Migration slide in your deck

Factor #1

The Great Migration 1916 to 1930

Black Southerners wanted paying work and a place where the law might apply to them.

The carried over 1.5 million Black Americans out of the rural South and into northern and industrial cities between 1916 and 1930. The war had shut off European immigration and opened up factory jobs, and the Chicago Defender ran train schedules alongside the argument for going.

Chicago's Black population went from about 44,000 in 1910 to more than 109,000 by 1920. The city did not build anything to hold them. Newcomers were packed into a narrow strip on the South Side at rents higher than white tenants paid for better rooms, and when Black families tried to move past the edge of that strip, their new houses were bombed.

White workers, many of them recent immigrants themselves, looked at the same jobs and decided the newcomers were the reason wages were what they were.

The 369th arriving in New York, from the World War One deck

Factor #2

The Veterans Came Home 1919

They wanted the country to mean what it had said to them in 1917.

Roughly 380,000 Black Americans served in World War One, in segregated units under white officers, and about 200,000 of them went to France. The 369th spent 191 days in the front line, longer than any other American regiment, and never lost a foot of ground or a man taken prisoner. France gave the whole regiment the .

They came back to a country where they could be beaten for wearing the uniform they had earned it in. There were no jobs held for them and no houses. In May 1919 W. E. B. Du Bois wrote in that they should return fighting, and that year, in Washington and Chicago and Omaha, Black communities did.

That is the part of 1919 that was new. White had attacked Black neighborhoods for decades. What changed was how often the neighborhoods shot back.

The nine men above were photographed on February 12, 1919, waiting to come ashore in New York, wearing the Croix de Guerre. Back row: Henry Davis Primas Senior, Daniel W. Storms Junior, Joe Williams, Alfred S. Manley, Tyler William Taylor. Front row: Ed Williams, Herbert Taylor, Leon E. Fraiter, Ralph Hawkins. For most of a century they were captioned as nobody in particular.

Joseph Hirsch (American, 1910–1981), Lynch Family, 1946. Oil on canvas, 35 × 33 in. (88.9 × 83.8 cm). Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, Kansas City, Missouri.

Factor #3

Lynching, and a Congress That Would Not Act 1918 to 1924

White mobs wanted the last word, and they were confident nobody would take it from them.

was still routine in 1919 and it was public. There were 64 recorded lynchings in 1918 and 83 in 1919, and at least ten of the men killed in 1919 were veterans, some of them still in uniform. Almost nobody was ever tried for any of it.

In April 1919 the published a study of thirty years of lynchings showing that fewer than one in six of the victims had even been accused of rape, which was the reason white mobs gave the country for what they did.

Congress had a bill in front of it. Representative Leonidas Dyer of Missouri had introduced an anti lynching bill in 1918 that would have made lynching a federal crime and fined the counties that allowed it. The House passed it on January 26, 1922, by 230 votes to 119. Southern senators it in 1922, in 1923 and again in 1924. It never became law. No federal anti lynching law passed until 2022.

Section 3

When and Where

Thirteen stops. Where it happened, and when. Watch the line fill in.

1of 13 events
July 1917

The warning nobody acted on

East St. Louis, Illinois

White went through Black neighborhoods for two days, shooting people and burning houses with families still inside. The official count was 39 Black dead and 9 white. Black witnesses and the put the real number far higher. The trigger was the same one that would keep working in 1919: Black workers had come north for jobs in the war plants.

July 28, 1917

The Silent Protest Parade

New York, New York

Thousands of Black New Yorkers walked down Fifth Avenue without saying a word, to the sound of muffled drums, the women and children in white. They carried a banner asking the president why he would not make America safe for democracy. The NAACP organized it in response to East St. Louis. It was the first protest march of its kind in the country.

December 11, 1917

Thirteen hanged before sunrise

Houston, Texas

After a night of violence in Houston touched off by police beating a Black woman and then a Black soldier who asked about it, the Army the men of the 24th Infantry in batches. Thirteen were hanged at once at dawn on December 11. They were not told when or where it would happen, and no court reviewed the sentences first. Six more were executed the following year. This is what Black soldiers knew about military justice when they shipped out for France.

February 17, 1919

The 369th comes home

New York, New York

The Hellfighters marched from 34th Street up Fifth Avenue, past the reviewing stand at 60th, and on to 145th and Lenox in Harlem, seven miles in tight French formation behind Lieutenant James Reese Europe's band. Hundreds of thousands of people lined the route. Sergeant Henry Johnson, too badly wounded to march, rode in an open car holding an armful of lilies. Five months later the same country produced the rest of this map.

May 10, 1919

Sailors in the streets

Charleston, South Carolina

White sailors from the naval base went into Charleston's Black neighborhoods after a fight over a dice game, joined by a white crowd. Isaac Doctor, William Brown and James Talbot were killed. The Navy eventually admitted its men had started it. was declared. This was the first of the 1919 attacks.

July 1919

The price of writing it down

Longview, Texas

A Black teacher named Samuel L. Jones was believed to have sent the Chicago Defender an account of a local that contradicted the white version of it. A mob beat him, then came back at night and burned Black homes and businesses. At least four people were killed. Longview is a reminder that in 1919 telling the truth about a lynching in print was itself dangerous.

July 19 to 24, 1919

Four days in the capital

Washington, District of Columbia

White servicemen, stirred up by weeks of lurid newspaper stories about Black attackers, began pulling Black people off streetcars and beating them in the street. On the second day the Washington Post printed a notice on the front page calling every available service man to assemble on Pennsylvania Avenue for a clean up. The police did not stop any of it. Black Washington armed itself, held its own blocks around Seventh and U, and fought for four days. Fifteen people died and ten of them were white, which had almost never happened before. President Wilson sent 2,000 federal troops on the fourth day, and a rainstorm did more to end it than they did.

July 27 to August 3, 1919

Thirteen days

Chicago, Illinois

A seventeen year old named Eugene Williams drifted across an invisible line in Lake Michigan and was stoned until he drowned. The police refused to arrest the man the Black witnesses pointed to, and arrested a Black man instead. Thirteen days later 38 people were dead, 23 of them Black, more than 500 were injured, and about 1,000 Black families had been burned out of their homes. See the section below.

August 30 and 31, 1919

The mob storms the jail

Knoxville, Tennessee

A white crowd broke into the Knox County jail to lynch a Black man accused of killing a white woman. He had already been moved out of the city, so the mob looted the jail, freed the white prisoners, and turned on Knoxville's Black business district instead. National Guardsmen fired a machine gun down Vine Avenue. At least seven people were killed and the real number is probably higher.

September 11, 1919

The president says he is ashamed

Helena, Montana

Wilson was crossing the country selling the League of Nations when he stopped mid speech in Helena to say that he wanted to express his shame as an American citizen at the race that had occurred in this country, where men had forgotten humanity and justice and orderly society and had run amuck. That was the whole of it. He had segregated the federal workforce six years earlier, he had refused the calls for a federal investigation, and he went on insisting that this was a matter for local authorities. Three weeks later he had a stroke and there was no federal response at all.

September 28 and 29, 1919

They burned the courthouse down

Omaha, Nebraska

A crowd that grew to thousands surrounded the Douglas County Courthouse demanding a Black packinghouse worker named Will Brown, held on an accusation. They siphoned gasoline from a filling station, poured it through the lower floors and set the building on fire with the police and prisoners still inside. When Mayor Edward Smith came out and told them no, they beat him with a bat, put a rope around his neck and hung him from a traffic signal tower. He was cut down alive. Will Brown was not. Federal troops arrived at three in the morning, and by the next day there were 1,600 soldiers and machine guns in the streets of Omaha. The photograph at the top of this page is that courthouse.

September 30 to October 2, 1919

The deadliest, and it was not a city

Elaine, Arkansas

Black in Phillips County met at a church in Hoop Spur to organize the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America, which wanted an honest accounting for the cotton the planters sold on their behalf. Shots were fired outside the meeting and a white railroad agent was killed. Hundreds of armed white men, and then federal troops, swept the county. Five white men died. Estimates of the Black dead run from scores into the hundreds and no one counted. Then 122 Black people were charged, and twelve were tried and sentenced to death in trials that took under an hour each. Nobody was charged for the killings. Ida B. Wells went to Phillips County herself, interviewed the condemned men in prison and published what she found, and the NAACP lawyer Scipio Jones fought the cases all the way to the Supreme Court, and won. In , decided on February 19, 1923, the Court threw out the death sentences and held that a trial run under the threat of a mob is no trial at all and denies the accused . It is the one lasting thing the produced.

May 31 and June 1, 1921

Greenwood

Tulsa, Oklahoma

Two years later, in Tulsa, a white mob destroyed the Greenwood district after Black veterans went to the courthouse to stop a lynching. More than ten blocks of Black homes were burned to the ground. It is on the next slide in your deck, and it belongs on this map.

PBS American Experience: how Red Summer led to Tulsa

Section 4

Chicago In Depth

One stop out of fifteen, and the one your textbook usually stops at.

It was ninety six degrees in Chicago on Sunday, July 27, 1919, and the beaches along the South Side were full. The Twenty Ninth Street beach was for white swimmers and the Twenty Fifth Street beach was for Black swimmers. No ordinance said so. Everyone knew it anyway.

Eugene Williams, seventeen, was in the water on a homemade raft with four friends. The raft drifted south of the invisible line. A group of white men on the breakwater threw stones. One hit him and he went under and drowned.

A Black crowd on the beach pointed out the man who had thrown the stone to Officer Daniel Callahan. He refused to arrest him. He arrested a Black man instead, on an unrelated complaint from a white bystander, while people were still pulling the body out of the lake.

The fighting ran thirteen days. The state was not called in until the fourth. When it stopped on August 3, 38 people were dead, 23 of them Black and 15 white, and more than 500 were injured, about two thirds of them Black. Roughly 1,000 Black families had been burned out of their homes and had nowhere to go back to.

The city then did something unusual. It created the , six white members and six Black, which spent two years on the question and published The Negro in Chicago in 1922. The Commission found that most of the violence had been started by white athletic clubs, several of them sponsored by ward politicians, and that the police had left them alone to do it. The Commission recommended better housing, fair hiring and even handed policing. The city built instead, which by 1925 were being written into deeds to keep Black families out of white blocks by contract.

A footnote with a long shadowOne of those white athletic clubs was the Hamburg Athletic Club, and one of its members in the summer of 1919 was a seventeen year old named Richard J. Daley, who would run Chicago from 1955 until he died in 1976. The Commission named the club. Daley was never asked in public what he did that week, and he never said.
